en: Let us go, children of the Fatherland!
The day of glory has arrived.
Do you hear in the countryside
They come right into our arms
To cut the throats of your sons, your companions!…
To arms, citizens! form your battalions.
Let us march (bis), may an impure blood water our furrows!
What does this horde of slaves want,
Frenchmen! for us, ah! what an outrage!
It is we whom they dare to plan
To return to the ancient slavery…
Would make the law in our homes!
Would strike down our proud warriors! (bis)
Our brows would bend beneath the yoke;
Tremble, tyrants! and you, treacherous ones,
Are at last going to receive their due. (bis)
Everyone is a soldier to fight you.
If they fall, our young heroes,
Against you, all ready to fight
Strike or hold back your blows.
Arming themselves against us with regret. (bis)
All these tigers who without pity
Tear the breast of their mother.
To arms, citizens! form your battalions.
Let us march (bis); may all their blood water our furrows!
See your triumph and our glory.
notes: General: this is the 1792 text of six stanzas; the 'children's stanza' ('Nous entrerons dans la carrière') was added later and is not in it. 'enfans' is the period spelling of 'enfants'. '(bis)' and 'etc.' are the source's repeat signs, kept as they stand.

line 1.10: 'qu'un sang impur abreuve nos sillons' — 'impure blood' is read by most historians as the enemies' (the invaders'); its exact sense is disputed and has been argued over since. Translated word for word.
lines 1.3-1.4: the word order of the original is kept ('Against us, of tyranny / the bloody standard is raised' = the bloody standard of tyranny is raised against us).
line 1.8: 'compagnes' are female companions, i.e. wives.
line 2.6: printed with a question mark in the source; 'transports' here means outbursts of feeling (fury, passion). Rendered as an exclamation.
lines 2.7-2.8: one sentence across two lines: 'it is we whom they dare to plan to return to the ancient slavery'.
lines 3.5-3.6: one sentence: 'by chained hands our brows would bend beneath the yoke'; the source's full stop after 'enchainées' is not followed.
line 4.1: the source prints 'Tremble' (not 'Tremblez') though tyrants are addressed in the plural.
line 5.2: Bouillé: François Claude, Marquis de Bouillé, the general who crushed the Nancy mutiny of 1790 and organised the king's flight to Varennes in 1791.
line 5.8: 'their mother' is the Fatherland, France.
line 5.9: the source prints 'forme ;' — a misprint for 'formez', translated as such.
line 6.6: 'tes mâles accents' — the manly (virile) voice or strains of Liberty.
